title: Trump 'Kamala Is for They/Them, I Am for You' — Systematic Transgender Attacks
description_short: Trump 'Kamala Is for They/Them, I Am for You' — Systematic Transgender Attacks
description_medium: Donald Trump’s 2024 campaign used the slogan “Kamala is for they/them, President Trump is for you” in television ads attacking Kamala Harris over transgender policy. The ads highlighted her past support for publicly funded gender-affirming care for incarcerated people, while using that narrow issue as a campaign contrast. CBS News reported the campaign spent $19 million airing the ads nearly 55,000 times from October 1 through 16, 2024.
description_long: During the 2024 presidential campaign, Donald Trump’s campaign made transgender policy a prominent attack line against Kamala Harris. Its television ad used the slogan “Kamala is for they/them, President Trump is for you” and featured Harris’s earlier support for publicly funded gender-affirming surgery for prisoners. The underlying position concerned care for incarcerated people; the ad presented it as a broader contrast between Harris and Trump. The message appeared in several versions and was heavily scheduled in battleground states, including during professional and college football broadcasts. CBS News reported that the campaign paid about $19 million to air the ad nearly 55,000 times between October 1 and October 16, 2024. The campaign’s repetition made transgender rights and health care a high-visibility election issue. The short slogan and frequent placement gave voters a simple contrast, while the specific policy at its center concerned a narrow question about care in prisons. The ad became one of the campaign’s most recognizable messages and kept that dispute in front of voters during the final weeks of the race.

title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia Deported Despite Court Protection Order
description_short: Kilmar Abrego Garcia Deported Despite Court Protection Order
description_medium: In March 2025, the Trump administration deported Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Maryland resident from El Salvador, despite a court order barring his removal to that country. He was sent to El Salvador’s CECOT prison. A federal judge later ordered officials to facilitate his return, and on April 10 the Supreme Court upheld that instruction. The administration argued it could not retrieve him from Salvadoran custody, making the case a test of compliance with court orders.
description_long: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national living in Maryland, was deported to El Salvador in March 2025 and held at the CECOT prison. A prior court order had barred his removal to El Salvador because of the danger he faced there. The administration later acknowledged that his deportation had been an error, but said it could not bring him back once he was in Salvadoran custody. A federal judge ordered the government to facilitate his return. On April 10, the Supreme Court upheld that requirement, directing the administration to take steps to secure his release and return. The dispute put the administration’s immigration enforcement against a specific judicial protection and raised a direct question about whether officials would carry out a court’s order after a person had been sent abroad. Abrego Garcia’s case became a prominent test of the limits of executive power and the ability of federal courts to enforce their rulings. The government’s position that it could not secure his release sharpened the conflict between its control over immigration enforcement and the court’s instruction.

title: Trump Pardons Oath Keepers and Proud Boys Leaders Convicted of Seditious Conspiracy
description_short: Trump Pardons Oath Keepers and Proud Boys Leaders Convicted of Seditious Conspiracy
description_medium: On January 20, 2025, Donald Trump issued sweeping clemency for people convicted in connection with the January 6 Capitol attack, including leaders of the Oath Keepers and Proud Boys. The action included pardons and sentence commutations, which released or reduced the sentences of people convicted of seditious conspiracy. Among those affected were Kelly Meggs, Joseph Biggs, and Zachary Rehl. The clemency ended federal punishment for conduct prosecutors had spent years investigating.
description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump issued clemency for roughly 1,500 people charged or convicted in connection with the January 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol. The action included both pardons and sentence commutations, so recipients did not all receive the same relief. It covered leaders and members of the Oath Keepers and Proud Boys who had been convicted of seditious conspiracy or related offenses. Kelly Meggs, Joseph Biggs, and Zachary Rehl were among those whose sentences were affected. Their prosecutions followed years of federal investigation into organized efforts surrounding the attack. The clemency took effect on Trump’s first day back in office and changed the legal consequences facing people convicted in the cases. Pardons ended punishment for their recipients, while commutations reduced sentences without erasing convictions. The decision released some people from custody and shortened the terms of others. It was a consequential use of presidential clemency for defendants whose cases arose from an effort to disrupt Congress’s certification of the 2020 election.

title: HHS Begins 10,000-Employee Layoff Affecting FDA, CDC, NIH and Other Agencies
description_short: HHS Begins 10,000-Employee Layoff Affecting FDA, CDC, NIH and Other Agencies
description_medium: On April 1, 2025, the Trump administration began layoffs affecting roughly 10,000 employees across HHS agencies, including the FDA, CDC and NIH. FDA scientists and senior officials were among those affected, but the 10,000 figure applied across the department rather than to FDA alone. The stored claim therefore substantially overstates FDA-specific cuts and uses the wrong month.
description_long: On April 1, 2025, HHS began layoffs affecting roughly 10,000 employees across its agencies, including the FDA, CDC, and NIH. The figure covered the department and did not mean that the FDA alone lost 10,000 people. Most agency staff were placed on leave as programs were cut. FDA scientists and senior officials were among those affected. The agencies have different duties: the FDA oversees food and medicines, the CDC conducts disease surveillance and prevention, and the NIH supports biomedical research. A single department-wide total combined workforce changes across these functions and did not show how many staff left each agency. The layoffs formed part of a broader restructuring of HHS. Employees across regulatory, public-health, and research agencies were affected by the same action, with different staffing impacts in each. The cuts changed staffing levels across the department but did not formally terminate the FDA, CDC, NIH, or the federal health department.
